name: Software engineering: test-based repair of the QuixBugs Python programs
description: Write a general repair procedure that receives a buggy QuixBugs Python program with a few visible tests and returns a patch of at most two statements. A patch counts only when it also passes held-out QuixBugs tests and generated tests whose expected outputs come from the reference fix.

sources.locator: Lin, Koppel, Chen and Solar-Lezama (SPLASH Companion 2017): the QuixBugs benchmark of 40 programs with one-line bugs in Python and Java.
Pinned QuixBugs commit (MIT licence): python_programs, correct_python_programs (used only at preparation time) and json_testcases.
Le Goues, Nguyen, Forrest and Weimer (TSE 2012): GenProg, test-suite-based generate-and-validate repair.
Smith, Barr, Le Goues and Brun (ESEC/FSE 2015): patches that pass the repair tests but fail held-out tests (overfitting).
Ye, Martinez, Durieux and Monperrus (JSS 2021): repair tools on QuixBugs; plausible patches checked for overfitting with generated tests.

requirements.datasets: QuixBugs at commit 4257f44b (MIT), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py; the reference fixes are used only to derive held-out tests and are not stored.

evaluation.benchmark: Software engineering: test-based repair of the QuixBugs Python programs
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: repair(task) -> str. task = {'name': str, 'entry': str, 'source': str, 'tests': [{'input': [arguments], 'expected': value, 'tolerance': float (only for sqrt)}, ...], 'max_statement_edits': 2}: 'source' is a buggy QuixBugs Python program defining the function 'entry'; 'tests' are its visible tests, at least one of which fails. Return the patched program as a str of at most 20000 characters that differs from 'source' in at most 2 statements (replaced, inserted or deleted statements of the parsed program; formatting and comments do not count). A test passes when entry(*input) returns the expected value after JSON normalisation (generators are consumed into lists, tuples become lists), or a number within 'tolerance' of it, within the test's step limit. A step is one function entry or one loop iteration of the program, counted by the evaluator, so the limit does not depend on the speed of the machine: 2,000,000 steps per test, and 25,000,000 for the test levenshtein('rosettacode', 'raisethysword'), on which the reference fix makes 10,308,990 calls (on every other test the reference fixes need at most 761,717 steps). A CPU-time limit of 10 s plus 2 microseconds per allowed step remains as a safety net for programs whose steps are individually slow. Score: fraction of the 31 programs whose patch passes its visible tests, its remaining QuixBugs tests and 10 to 40 generated held-out tests whose expected values come from the reference fix (higher is better); a patch passing only some of them counts as overfitting, not repaired. repair() runs once per program in a sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 4 s CPU, 1 GB) and may execute the given program and tests itself; it should be deterministic. The procedure must be general: remembered program-specific fixes are outside the contract. A repair() call that raises, exceeds its limits or returns something other than a str of at most 20000 characters makes the whole evaluation invalid.

limitations: Uses the 31 Python programs with JSON tests; the nine graph programs are excluded, so results reported on all 40 programs are not comparable, nor are results of tools that call language models.

Correctness is decided by tests: the visible tests, the remaining QuixBugs tests and 10 to 40 generated inputs per program checked against the reference fix. A semantically different but test-equivalent patch counts as a repair, and a wrong patch that agrees on all these inputs would also count; there is no manual patch review.
Generated inputs respect the documented preconditions and avoid inputs whose correct output is not unique; inputs on which the reference fix itself loops (some wrap cases) are excluded.
The programs and their fixes are public, so a candidate could embed remembered fixes; the contract excludes this but it cannot be checked automatically.
Each repair() call gets 4 s of CPU time in a Python sandbox, far less than the hours given to repair tools in the literature.

The suite's evaluator template imports the candidate module in the evaluator process before scoring; every scored call runs in the sandbox, which cannot read the held-out data, but deliberately hostile import-time code could. Untrusted evaluations should run in a container without the prepared files.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published result uses this 31-program subset with these held-out tests. Ye et al. (2021) report repair tools on all 40 Java QuixBugs programs, and language-model studies report counts on all 40 Python programs under other correctness criteria.

sources.title: A comprehensive study of automatic program repair on the QuixBugs benchmark

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Automated program repair: given a faulty program and tests that expose the fault, produce a small patch that makes the program correct, not merely one that passes the given tests.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Debugging consumes a large share of development effort; test-suite-based repair is one of the most studied routes to automating it, and patch overfitting to the available tests is its central open difficulty.

papers.title: GenProg: A Generic Method for Automatic Software Repair
papers.primary_goal: Automatically repair defects in real programs by searching for patches that make the failing tests pass while keeping the passing ones.
papers.task_relation: The task asks for the same kind of procedure: a test-guided repair of a buggy program.

papers.title: Is the cure worse than the disease? Overfitting in automated program repair
papers.primary_goal: Measure how often automatically generated patches overfit the tests used for repair, using independent held-out tests.
papers.task_relation: The task separates repaired from overfitting patches with held-out tests in the same way.

papers.title: A comprehensive study of automatic program repair on the QuixBugs benchmark
papers.primary_goal: Assess how well repair tools fix the QuixBugs programs and how many of their plausible patches are actually correct.
papers.task_relation: The task uses the QuixBugs programs and judges correctness beyond the original tests.
